newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Twenty-four Timorese charged with showing hatred.
newsitem.headline: Twenty-four Timorese charged with showing hatred.

text.p: Police said on Tuesday they had charged 24 East Timorese with showing hatred against the Indonesian government after they staged a protest during a visit by the U.N. special envoy for East Timor, Jamsheed Marker.

"We have released 24 people but still detain 24 others. They have been charged with publicly showing hatred against the government," East Timor deputy police chief Lieutenant-Colonel Atok Rismanto told Reuters from Dili, the capital of East Timor.
"The banners they displayed show hatred against the government," he added. Showing hatred carries a maximum penalty of seven years in jail.
On Sunday, a group of youths, mainly students, demonstrated at the Mahkota Hotel in Dili where Marker was staying. At least 48 of them were arrested after brief scuffles.
Marker, who flew back to Jakarta on Monday after a three-day visit in East Timor, said he was in his room at the time of the demonstration and did not see what happened.
Rismanto said the 24 people were also accused of property damage, possessing sharp weapons and resisting arrest, adding that no one was killed when police dispersed the protest.
"No one was killed. We will say it if there is a death...because no matter how clever we are in telling lies, people will later find out the truth," he said. Rismanto gave no further details.
Police earlier said they had seized 12 machetes and knives and 19 banners in Sunday's demonstration and that 11 people were injured.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Marker as special envoy for East Timor last month in an effort to swiftly resolve a row between Indonesia and Portugal over the territory.

Residents in Dili said demonstrators tried to meet Marker after they felt frustrated that he was meeting only with government officials and Bishop Carlos Belo. Marker denied he had refused to meet the students, saying they had not asked for a meeting.

Indonesia invaded East Timor with tacit Western support in December 1975 after the abrupt withdrawal of Portuguese colonial authorities. Indonesia declared the territory its 27th province the following July in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
